newsitem.title: MEXICO: Volatility seen hitting Mexico primary Cetes rates.
newsitem.headline: Volatility seen hitting Mexico primary Cetes rates.

text.p: Mexico's primary Cetes rates could push up another notch or two at Banco de Mexico's Treasury bill auction next week as nervous investors react to a number of temporary problems hitting Mexico, analysts said on Thursday.
The size of the increase, following a 458-basis-point rise in the bellwether one-month paper in the last two auctions, will depend on how political factors unwind, they said.
But a clearly stronger economic picture will help keep rates more stable at the longer-end of the yield curve, they noted.
"There are a number of transitory factors that have caused the sharp rise in the short end, but we see it as a temporary correction," said Arka Brokerage economist Esteban Rojas.

Among the factors is ongoing political tension over the process in the United States of certifying whether Mexico has been fighting drug trafficking with enough vigour. On Thursday, the U.S. House of Representatives voted to give Mexico 90 days to improve its performance in the drug war.
Added to that are worries over whether the U.S. Federal Reserve will sanction an interest rate hike at its Open Market Committee Meeting (FOMC) on March 25.
A sharp rise in the yield on the U.S. 30-year bond has added to the pressure on Mexican rates as well.
"I think that the big fear is that next week's auction will come before the next FOMC meeting in March," said one money market dealer who declined to be identified.
Another market analyst said that he expects a rise of between 100 and 150 basis points in Mexican one-month Cetes rates next week.
Arka's Rojas said he sees rates resuming a downward trend at least from April.
The volatility in Mexican rates has been seen most clearly in the short end of the Cetes yield curve, but not as much in the long end where economic issues are a bigger factor, analysts said.
For example, at the primary auction this week, the one-month paper rate rose a sharp 201 basis points to yield 23.17 percent, following a 257-basis point rise the week before.
But rates on the three-month paper and the six-month paper rate were almost flat, while the one-year paper rate fell slightly.
The rebound in rates followed a 10-week slide to their lowest levels since the 1994 peso crash as investors looked out and saw waning inflationary pressures.

That trend was broken, however, by uncertainty in international markets, payments on Mexico's external debt, and the U.S. drug certification process that pressured the exchange rate and drove up interest rates, brokerage house MultiValores said in a report.
Those concerns over rising interest rates are reverberating.
For example, on Thursday, Deutsche Morgan Grenfell cut Mexico to short-term underweight from neutral in its Latin American stock portfolio due to among other things, the volatile fixed-income market.
Late Wednesday, leading business group spokesman Carlos Abascal said at a press conference that interest rates could rebound if U.S. rates rose, and to keep investors interested in Mexican paper.

"It wouldn't be strange if there was still another rebound in rates due to these two things that I mentioned: rates in the United States and (low) real rates for investors in Mexico," said Abascal, president of the Mexican Confederation of Employers (Coparmex).
((-- Mexico City newsroom 525 728-9559))
